Besteman 2

TrianglesConstructionsCircles
Game: Drag two dots and watch circles and a slanted line split a long segment into equal pieces.
How to play: Drag A or B with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Choose how many pieces you want, then press Check the claims.
Look for the math

Angle bisectors are usually used to cut angles in half. Bogomolny's second Besteman construction turns that fact around: it cuts a segment into any chosen number of equal parts, using only circles and one bisector.

A bisector compares two sides

In any triangle ACD, let DP be the angle bisector from D, meeting AC at P. Comparing the two smaller triangles by their heights and their shared half-angle gives the angle-bisector theorem:

AP / PC = AD / CD.

The two coloured arcs at D in the picture show that the two angles are equal. This is claim (1) on the original page, and it holds no matter where D is.

The second Besteman claim

Now make the side from D to C exactly m times the side from D to A: CD = m · AD. The theorem gives AP = PC/m, so PC = m · AP and the whole segment is AC = (m+1)·AP. That is the page's second claim, written there with N in place of m:

CD = N · AD  implies  AP = PC/N = AC/(N+1).

This is not the first Besteman construction. That older page uses a perpendicular chord and similar right triangles to get AP = AB²/(2AC), and chooses AC = N·AB/2 to make AP = AB/N — one Nth of the original segment AB. The second theorem instead uses the bisector and gives one Nth of the extended segment AC. For N = 2 both happen to find the midpoint; for N ≥ 3 they are different lengths.

What this applet draws

Here N means the number of equal parts. A and B are dragged along one horizontal line with AB = d; C is placed N−1 steps from A, so AC = (N−1)d. Two circles centred at A and C, of radii d and (N−1)d, meet at D. Therefore AD = d and CD = (N−1)d: this is the theorem above with m = N−1, giving AP = AC/N. The green dots are at A + k·AP for k = 0, …, N−1, with C as the last endpoint, so all N pieces are the same length.

The logic test checks every N from 2 to 20 and 80 random placements of A and B, in both directions. It also re-runs the applet's own arithmetic from its bytecode — circle intersection for D, rotate-and-intersect for the bisector foot — and compares every dot.

Try N = 2 first: the two circles have the same radius and P is the midpoint. Then press + a few times and watch C run off while the green dots stay evenly spaced.
